Question: A bag contains four pieces of paper, each labeled with one of the digits \(1,\) \(2,\) \(3\) or \(4,\) with no repeats. Three of these pieces are drawn, one at a time without replacement, to construct a three-digit number. What is the probability that the three-digit number is a multiple of \(3?\)
Solution:
Divisibility by \(3\) depends only on the sum of the digits, so their order does not affect whether the number wins. The four available digits sum to
\[
1+2+3+4=10.
\]
Omitting \(1,2,3,4\) gives digit sums \(9,8,7,6\), respectively. Only \(9\) and \(6\) are multiples of \(3\), so the favorable omitted digits are \(1\) and \(4\).

Each omitted digit leaves three distinct digits, which can be drawn in \(3\times2\times1=6\) orders. All these ordered draws are equally likely. Every draw omits exactly one digit, so the four groups are disjoint, exhaustive, and equal in size. There are no leading-zero exceptions because all available digits are nonzero.

Two of the four equally likely groups are favorable, giving probability
\[
\frac24=\boxed{\frac12},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
